claims.text: Repeated mechanical disruption of the protective passive layer is the primary driver of accelerated material loss under HEA tribo-corrosion.
Passive-layer disruption periodically exposes fresh, reactive alloy surfaces.
The newly exposed surfaces rapidly corrode and thereby deepen mechanical wear.
The proposed initial alloy is single-phase or near-single-phase.
The polished initial surface has a well-formed passive film.
Normal load and solution pH can be varied systematically while wear and electrochemical response are monitored in real time.
The governing structural mediator is the dynamic breakdown, re-formation, and repassivation of the contact-surface oxide or passive layer during sliding.
Increasing normal load intensifies mechanical disruption of near-surface oxide layers.
Acidic conditions intensify localized electrochemical activity.
Film disruption allows corrosive species to reach exposed metal and accelerates local dissolution.
Accelerated dissolution promotes debris formation.
Corrosion-generated debris enhances abrasive wear and causes further passive-film disruption.
Each increase in normal load and each decrease in pH will significantly increase total material loss relative to mild-load, neutral-pH conditions.
At the highest load and lowest pH, total material loss will exceed twice the baseline loss.
Mechanical wear without corrosive electrolyte and electrochemical corrosion without mechanical contact will each produce lower degradation than coupled tribo-corrosion.
Near-neutral pH and minimal load limit oxide-film disruption and total material loss.
Highly alkaline conditions or very low load minimize wear-corrosion synergy because stable passive films persist.
At extremely high loads, direct mechanical failure dominates rather than wear-corrosion synergy.
In strongly acidic media, uniform corrosion dominates rather than wear-corrosion synergy.
A verified, mechanically durable passive film producing the same or greater total loss as an unprotected surface would contradict passive-film disruption as the primary degradation driver.
